category: PCB Layout (ARES): board setup, placement, routing & copper
description: Getting a Proteus PCB laid out: taking the live netlist from the schematic, defining the board edge, layer stackup and design rules with net classes and rooms, placing components manually or with the auto placer, follow-me push-and-shove manual routing, the shape-based autorouter, differential pairs and length matching, vias and drill spans, copper zones and power planes, and the copper clean-up tools.

tools.name: Netlist load from schematic (live netlist)
tools.description: In Proteus 8 and later the schematic and layout share one project database, so connectivity is passed live: drawing a wire immediately updates the ratsnest and deleting a part removes its footprint. Tools > Live Netlist toggles this off in favour of traditional batch netlisting, in which each netlist load is confirmed manually — useful on very large designs but it disables some menu commands until the netlist is back in sync.
tools.usage: Automatic in the PCB Layout tab; Tools > Live Netlist toggles between live and batch netlisting
tools.example: Wire a new connection on the schematic and switch to the PCB Layout tab — the ratsnest line is already there.
tools.notes: Deleting a component on the schematic with live netlisting on also deletes its footprint and its connected tracks; delete the package on the layout instead if you want the tracks left as stubs.

tools.name: Board edge definition
tools.description: The board outline is drawn as 2D graphics (usually a closed path or box) on the Board Edge layer. Everything downstream depends on it: the autoplacer and autorouter are bounded by it, zones are clipped to it, the 3D visualizer extrudes it, and the CADCAM output uses it as the profile.
tools.usage: Select the Board Edge layer in the layer selector, then use 2D Graphics Box / Closed Path mode to draw the outline
tools.example: Set the layer to Board Edge, 2D Graphics Box mode, draw a 80 x 50 mm rectangle, then place components inside it.
tools.notes: Import a mechanical outline instead with File > Import > DXF onto the Board Edge layer when the enclosure defines the shape.

tools.name: Layer Stackup Wizard
tools.description: Defines the board's construction: the number and order of copper layers, the dielectric and core thicknesses and materials, and — for HDI designs — the 1+n+1 build-up with laser-drilled micro-via spans. Proteus supports boards of up to 16 copper layers, with the available count depending on the licensed product configuration.
tools.usage: Technology > Set Layer Stackup… (the Stackup Wizard); drill spans are configured alongside the stackup

parameters.name: Layer count
parameters.description: Number of copper layers, up to 16 depending on the product configuration.

parameters.name: Material / thickness per layer
parameters.description: Core and prepreg construction, used for impedance and for the 3D view.

parameters.name: Drill spans
parameters.description: Which layer pairs a via may span — through, blind, buried and laser-drilled micro vias.

parameters.name: 1+n+1 HDI
parameters.description: High-density build-up with micro-via layers on each face.

tools.example: Technology > Set Layer Stackup > 4 layers, 1.6 mm total, inner layers as planes; add a blind drill span from Top to Inner1 for the BGA escape.

tools.name: Design Rule Manager
tools.description: Proteus's constraint system. The Design Rules tab starts from a board-global rule giving the base clearances (pad-pad, pad-trace, trace-trace, graphics, edge) and lets additional rules be added for specific layers, specific net classes or specific regions (design rule rooms). The Net Classes tab gives each group of signals its own trace style, via style and routing preferences, which both the manual router and the autorouter obey.
tools.usage: Technology > Design Rule Manager… (tabs: Design Rules, Net Classes, and the region/room rules)

parameters.name: Region
parameters.description: Whole board, a named layer, or a design rule room covering part of the board.

parameters.name: Clearances
parameters.description: Pad-to-pad, pad-to-trace, trace-to-trace, graphics and edge clearances.

parameters.name: Net class trace style
parameters.description: Default trace width for the class, used automatically when routing its nets.

parameters.name: Net class via style
parameters.description: Via padstack, and whether routing must use through-hole vias or may use the shortest legal drill span.

parameters.name: Priority
parameters.description: More specific rules override the board-global rule.

tools.example: Design Rule Manager > add a room rule under the BGA with 0.15 mm clearances; Net Classes > POWER > trace style 'T40', via style 'V60'.
tools.notes: Set the rules before placement and routing: the follow-me router and the autorouter both derive their behaviour from them.

tools.name: Design rule rooms
tools.description: Rectangular regions of the board in which a different design rule applies, so a fine-pitch BGA area can use tighter clearances than the rest of the board, or a high-voltage section can demand a much larger one. Rooms are drawn on the layout and referenced by a rule in the Design Rule Manager.
tools.usage: Draw the room region on the board, then add a rule scoped to it in Technology > Design Rule Manager
tools.example: Draw a room over the BGA, add a rule with 0.1 mm trace-trace clearance inside it while the board default stays at 0.2 mm.

tools.name: Grid and units
tools.description: Sets the snap grid and the working units (imperial or metric). Proteus offers several selectable snap steps plus a real-time snap to pads and track ends; getting the grid right for the dominant component pitch is what makes placement and routing land accurately.
tools.usage: View > Snap (grid options) and the grid buttons; System > Set Units / the metric-imperial toggle
tools.example: Switch to metric, set the snap to 0.1 mm for routing a 0.5 mm-pitch QFN, then back to 0.5 mm for placement.

tools.name: Component placement (manual)
tools.description: Footprints arrive in the Components bin after the netlist is loaded and are placed by selecting one and clicking on the board. While a package is on the cursor it can be rotated and mirrored, and the ratsnest shows its connections live so it can be positioned against its connectivity. Cross-probing from the schematic selects the matching package.
tools.usage: Select the package in the Components bin (object selector) > click on the board; use the rotate/mirror buttons while placing
tools.example: Click U1 in the bin, rotate it 90°, place it in the centre of the board, and watch the ratsnest re-fan as it moves.

tools.name: Auto Placer
tools.description: Places the unplaced components automatically inside the board edge, using the connectivity to group related parts and a set of weighting options for grid, rotation and the trade-off between routability and density. It produces a starting arrangement that is then refined by hand, not a finished placement.
tools.usage: Tools > Auto Placer…; set the placement grid, rotation options and the design-rule-driven spacing
tools.example: Tools > Auto Placer > include all unplaced components, grid 0.5 mm, allow 90° rotations > OK, then tidy the result manually.

tools.name: Ratsnest and force vectors
tools.description: The ratsnest draws the unrouted connections as straight lines and re-computes as parts move. Force vectors show, for a selected component, the direction in which its connections are pulling it, which is a quick numerical guide to a better position during manual placement.
tools.usage: View > Ratsnest options; select a component and enable force vectors to see the pull direction
tools.example: Select the decoupling capacitor and enable force vectors — the arrow points at the IC's supply pin, confirming it should sit closer.

tools.name: Track Mode (follow-me manual routing)
tools.description: Proteus's manual router. Clicking on a pad picks up that pad's net and automatically selects the trace style from the net class; dragging the mouse draws the track of best fit that obeys the design rules (the 'follow me' behaviour), a left click places an anchor, and a left click on the destination pad commits the route. Push-and-shove moves existing tracks aside as you route.
tools.usage: Track Mode on the left toolbar; click the source pad, drag, click to anchor, click the destination pad to finish

parameters.name: Trace style
parameters.description: Width selected automatically from the net class, or chosen manually in the object selector.

parameters.name: Follow-me routing
parameters.description: Auto-computes a legal path towards the cursor as you drag.

parameters.name: Push and shove
parameters.description: Existing tracks are moved aside to make room rather than blocking the route.

tools.example: Track Mode, click the MCU's RB0 pad — Proteus picks up the net and its style — drag towards the LED, click the LED pad to commit.
tools.notes: Double-clicking a pad with Track Mode active places a via or starts the route on the other layer, depending on the current layer selection.

tools.name: Curved tracks and trace angle lock
tools.description: Proteus can route with curved (arc) track segments as well as the usual 45° and 90° angles, which is used for RF and for aesthetic or mechanically constrained routing. The angle lock setting constrains new segments to the chosen increments so routing stays tidy.
tools.usage: Track Mode options / right-click the track mode button for the angle and curve settings
tools.example: Enable curved tracks and route the antenna feed as a smooth arc rather than two 45° segments.

tools.name: Via placement and drill spans
tools.description: A via is placed by changing layer while routing, or explicitly with Via Mode. Which spans are legal comes from the layer stackup's drill definitions, and the net class decides whether routing must use through-hole vias or may use the shortest legal span (blind, buried or laser micro via).
tools.usage: Via Mode on the left toolbar, or change the current layer while routing; via styles come from the net class or the object selector
tools.example: While routing on the top layer, switch to the bottom layer — Proteus drops a via of the net class's style and continues on the new layer.

tools.name: Shape-based autorouter
tools.description: Proteus's built-in autorouter, included as standard with every PCB product. It routes the whole board, selected nets or the remaining unrouted connections using the current design rules and net classes, with strategy settings for pass counts, via costs and layer direction bias. It is best used for the non-critical majority after the important nets have been routed by hand.
tools.usage: Tools > Auto Router… > choose the scope and strategy > Begin Routing

parameters.name: Routing scope
parameters.description: All connections, selected nets/classes, or only those not already routed.

parameters.name: Protect existing tracks
parameters.description: Stops the router ripping up manual routing.

parameters.name: Strategy / pass settings
parameters.description: Effort, via cost and layer bias controls.

tools.example: Route the power and clocks by hand, lock them, then Tools > Auto Router > 'Route all unrouted' with 'protect existing' ticked.

tools.name: Differential pair routing
tools.description: A dedicated routing mode that draws both members of a differential pair together at the gap defined by their net class, and applies automatic skew correction so the intra-pair length mismatch introduced at breakouts and corners is removed without manual serpentine work.
tools.usage: Define the pair in the net class settings, then use the differential pair routing mode from the Track Mode options
tools.example: Assign USB_DP/USB_DN to a differential net class with the required gap, start the pair route at either pad, and let the automatic skew correction equalise the members.
tools.notes: Differential pair routing and length matching are features of the higher-tier PCB product levels, not of the entry configuration.

tools.name: Signal net tuning (group length matching)
tools.description: Matches routed net lengths either to each other within a group or to a specified target distance, adding serpentine to the short members. It is the tool for source-synchronous buses and memory byte lanes where skew, not just connectivity, determines whether the interface works.
tools.usage: Select the nets or net class and apply the length-matching/tuning command from the routing tools; set the group target or the explicit distance
tools.example: Select the eight data nets, choose match-to-longest with a 0.2 mm tolerance, and let Proteus add the serpentine to the short ones.

tools.name: Zone Mode (copper zones and power planes)
tools.description: Creates a filled copper area tied to a net. Zones automatically void around pads, tracks and vias of other nets, generate thermal relief or direct connections to their own net's pads according to the zone properties, and are clipped to the board edge. A zone on an inner layer with a supply net is how a power plane is made, and several net-assigned zones on one layer produce a split plane.
tools.usage: Zone Mode on the left toolbar > draw the boundary (or use the board edge) > set the net, layer, clearance, relief style and hatching in the zone dialog

parameters.name: Net
parameters.description: Net the zone connects to; an unassigned zone is floating copper.

parameters.name: Layer / Style
parameters.description: Copper layer and the trace style used for the boundary and hatching.

parameters.name: Relief / Thermal
parameters.description: Whether same-net pads get thermal spokes or a direct connection.

parameters.name: Clearance
parameters.description: Gap to objects of other nets, normally taken from the design rules.

parameters.name: Suppress islands
parameters.description: Removes copper fragments with no connection to the net.

tools.example: Zone Mode > draw over the whole bottom layer > net GND, thermal relief for through-hole pads, suppress islands > OK.
tools.notes: Zones regenerate when the design changes; regenerate them explicitly before producing CADCAM output so the plotted copper matches the screen.

tools.name: 2D graphics and silkscreen text
tools.description: The same 2D Graphics modes as the schematic (line, box, circle, arc, closed path, text, symbols), used on the layout for the board edge, silkscreen legends, assembly outlines, keep-out regions, mechanical notes and documentation. Each object belongs to a selected layer, which determines where it appears in the output.
tools.usage: 2D Graphics modes on the left toolbar with the target layer selected in the layer selector
tools.example: Select Top Silk, 2D Graphics Text mode, place 'REV B' and the polarity markings beside the connector.

tools.name: Measure and Move tool
tools.description: A precision positioning tool that measures a distance and moves the selected object by an exact amount, so components and features can be placed against dimensional requirements rather than by eye. Introduced with the Proteus 9.2 layout improvements.
tools.usage: PCB Layout > the Measure and Move tool; measure between two points and enter the required offset
tools.example: Measure from the board edge to the connector body and move the connector so the shell sits exactly 1.5 mm proud of the edge.

tools.name: Object grouping
tools.description: Groups layout objects so they move, rotate and are selected together — a connector with its mounting holes and keep-out, or a repeated sub-circuit with its routing. It keeps carefully arranged blocks intact while the rest of the board is rearranged.
tools.usage: Select the objects > the grouping command in the PCB Layout module (Proteus 9.2 and later)
tools.example: Group the RF front end's components, tracks and ground stitching so the whole block can be repositioned as one.

tools.name: Mitre and auto-mitre
tools.description: Replaces a sharp 90° track corner with a 45° chamfer or an arc, either on a selected corner or automatically across the board. It improves manufacturability and impedance behaviour and removes the acid-trap geometry that fabricators object to.
tools.usage: Right-click a track corner > Mitre; or the auto-mitre command to process the whole board
tools.example: Run auto-mitre after the autorouter finishes so no right-angle corners remain in the copper.

tools.name: Trace necking
tools.description: Locally narrows a track so it can pass between closely spaced pads or through a tight escape, while the rest of the net keeps its full width. The necked width is still checked against the design rules, so it cannot silently violate the minimum.
tools.usage: Select the track segment and apply the neck command, or route with a narrower trace style through the constriction
tools.example: Neck the 0.5 mm power track down to 0.25 mm to pass between two BGA pads, then return to full width.

tools.name: Teardrops
tools.description: Adds a tapered copper fillet where a track meets a pad or via, improving mechanical strength and drill-breakout tolerance. Teardrops are generated across the board (or a selection) and are regenerated after significant re-routing.
tools.usage: The teardrop command in the PCB Layout tools; apply after routing is complete
tools.example: Run the teardrop command once routing is final, then re-run the DRC to confirm no clearance was consumed.

tools.name: Copper thieving
tools.description: Fills large empty copper areas with a pattern of small isolated copper features so the board etches and plates evenly. Fabricators ask for it on boards with very uneven copper distribution, and Proteus generates it as a board-wide operation with a configurable pattern and clearance.
tools.usage: The copper thieving command in the PCB Layout module; set the pattern, size and clearance
tools.example: Apply copper thieving to the large blank area beside the connector before generating the CADCAM output.

tools.name: Round holes, slots and mounting holes
tools.description: Drill features are pads with a hole: plated pads for through-hole pins and grounded mounting holes, unplated pads for mechanical clearance holes, and slot-shaped pad styles for slotted or routed holes. Because they are pads they appear in the drill output and are checked by the design rules; a circle drawn on a silk or mechanical layer is not drilled.
tools.usage: Pad Mode with a pad style that has the required drill and plating; slots are defined in the pad style
tools.example: Place four unplated 3.2 mm pads at the corners for M3 clearance holes; the Excellon output lists them in the non-plated program.

tools.name: Layer visibility and board options
tools.description: Controls which layers are drawn, in which colours, and which is the current working layer, plus the board-level display options. On a dense multi-layer board this is the difference between a readable canvas and an unusable one, and it also determines what is included when an output area is printed.
tools.usage: View > Layers / the layer selector and colour configuration; Technology and System menus for the board display options
tools.example: Hide every layer except Top Copper and Top Silk while checking the silkscreen against the pads.

tools.name: Cross-probing with the schematic
tools.description: Selecting a component, pin or net in the PCB Layout module highlights the corresponding object on the schematic and vice versa, because both modules read the same project database. It is how a track is traced back to the circuit it belongs to during layout and debugging.
tools.usage: Open the Schematic Capture and PCB Layout tabs; select in either module
tools.example: Click a ratsnest line on the layout and the corresponding wire is highlighted on the schematic, showing which signal is still unrouted.
